title: Moment of Inertia of Continuous Rigid Bodies via Spatial Mass Integration
learning_objective: Calculate moment of inertia for standard continuous symmetric bodies by formulating differential mass elements dm and evaluating definite integrals.
explanation: For continuous mass distributions, summation over discrete particles passes into a definite volume integral: $$I = \int r_\perp^2 \, dm = \int r_\perp^2 \rho(ec{r}) \, dV$$ where $r_\perp$ represents the perpendicular distance of the differential mass element $dm$ from the designated rotation axis. For uniform densities, mass elements are formulated via geometric dimensions: linear mass density $dm = \lambda \, dl$ for thin rods, areal surface density $dm = \sigma \, dA$ for discs and planar sheets, and volumetric density $dm = \rho \, dV$ for cylinders and spheres. Standard integration results about central symmetry axes include: thin uniform rod of length $L$ about its perpendicular bisector ($I = \frac{1}{12} M L^2$), uniform circular ring ($I = M R^2$), uniform circular disc or solid cylinder ($I = \frac{1}{2} M R^2$), thin hollow spherical shell ($I = \frac{2}{3} M R^2$), and solid homogeneous sphere ($I = \frac{2}{5} M R^2$).
intuition: Moment of inertia measures how difficult it is to alter a body's angular velocity. Because mass elements contribute with the square of their radial distance from the axis ($r^2$), mass positioned far from the rotation axis contributes disproportionately more to rotational inertia than mass packed near the rotation axis.
formal_definition: The second moment of the mass distribution of a continuous rigid body with respect to a line axis $L$: $$I_L \equiv \iiint_V r_\perp^2 \rho(\vec{r}) \, dV$$ where $r_\perp$ is the Euclidean distance from the element $dV$ to the line $L$.
assumptions: Rigid body with invariant spatial distance between all constituent mass points
Homogeneous mass distribution with constant density
Specified geometric symmetry axes passing through centroid
boundary_conditions: Valid for macroscopic continuous rigid bodies in classical Newtonian mechanics
Fails for flexible, deformable, or non-rigid fluid media
source_references: H.C. Verma Vol 1, Chapter 10 (Rotational Mechanics), Sections 10.3-10.5
University Physics, Chapter 9 (Rotation of Rigid Bodies), Section 9.5
